item.title: NBA star Kyrie Irving jumps into NFL drama, offers to pay player's fine for Gaza-themed eye black
item.description: Kyrie Irving offered to cover Azeez Al-Shaair's $11,492 NFL fine for writing "Hind Rajab" on his eye black, marking his latest political gesture.
item.content:encoded:
Leave it to Kyrie Irving to find a brand-new way to play white knight in someone else’s political circus.

The Dallas Mavericks star is pulling out his wallet yet again, offering to cover the $11,492 fine handed down to Houston Texans linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair after he wrote "Hind Rajab," a five-year-old Palestinian girl killed in Gaza in 2024, on his eye black during Week 1 against the Buffalo Bills.

When the disciplinary report surfaced on X, Kyrie posted regarding Al-Shaair: "I’ll take care of his fine."

NFL RESTARTS SOCIAL JUSTICE MESSAGING WHILE BATTLING DOMESTIC ABUSE, DRUNK DRIVING AND PROSTITUTION ARRESTS

The NFL penalized Al-Shaair under strict rules banning unauthorized personal messages on game-day gear. And this is not his first offense.

In January 2026, he took an $11,593 hit for writing "Stop the Genocide" on his eye black during a playoff matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers. That is on top of his history of cheap shots on the field, including the brutal late hit on a sliding Trevor Lawrence that earned him a three-game suspension.

NFL PUTS 'INSPIRE CHANGE' AND 'CHOOSE LOVE' ON FIELDS BUT NOT SO AGGRESSIVE ABOUT ITS DOMESTIC ABUSE ISSUES

Between his vocal Muslim faith and his endless appetite for a spiritual crusade, Kyrie opening his wallet here surprises nobody.

In late 2022, while with the Brooklyn Nets, he sparked a massive firestorm by sharing a link to "Hebrews to Negroes: Wake Up Black America," a movie filled with antisemitic tropes, Holocaust denial and claims attributing the slave trade to Jewish people.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

After refusing to unequivocally disavow antisemitism, the Nets suspended Irving for eight games, declaring him "unfit to be associated" with the franchise. An Instagram apology eventually followed, but Kyrie’s habit of using his fortune to back unauthorized political statements clearly is not going anywhere.

Don't expect any nuance from NFL compliance officers.

That same week, Cardinals backup cornerback Kei’Trel Clark caught a $6,651 penalty simply for putting "Glory Be 2 God" and a peace symbol on his eye black against the Chargers. Clark accepted the penalty on Instagram, writing that he will always "give God the Glory and out loud."

Geopolitical protest or religious speech, the league seemingly treats all unauthorized eye-black messages the same.

item.title: Ohio mom of 16 cradles stomach in court, pleads not guilty in severe abuse case involving own children
item.description: Elizabeth Siders cradled her stomach in an orange jumpsuit while pleading not guilty to child sexual abuse and child endangerment charges in Ohio.
item.content:encoded:
An Ohio mother of 16 children who were rescued from a home where they allegedly lived in horrific conditions cradled her stomach while in court, where she pleaded not guilty Wednesday to the charges against her.

Elizabeth Siders, 34, who faces four counts of child sexual abuse and 19 counts of child endangerment, appeared in court, FOX 8 reported.

While in front of the judge, Siders, who was dressed in an orange jumpsuit, kept shielding her stomach and clutched her belly, The Daily Mail reported.

Fox News Digital has reached out to her attorney, Thomas Stolly, for comment on the charges against his client, as well as whether she is once again pregnant.

OHIO MOM ARRESTED FOR HAVING 16 KIDS IN 'EVIL' LIVING CONDITIONS WANTS TO BE REUNITED WITH CHILDREN: LAWYER

"We have an individual in Elizabeth who was married at age 15, who has essentially been pregnant for the better part of two decades," Stolly told local media. "Who has never fully gone through any postpartum period, who has not been receiving regular medical care that would be appropriate for someone who has had 16, 18 children."

"I have concerns about what effects those have had on her," he added.

HSI AGENT WHO INVESTIGATED CHILD EXPLOITATION CASES INDICTED ON RAPE AND CHILD ABUSE CHARGES

Siders and her husband, Gary Siders Jr., are accused of sexual abuse against a minor in 2022. The alleged victim is not among the 16 children, the news report states.

However, the child was in the care of the couple at the time the alleged abuse occurred. Gary Siders Jr. has also pleaded not guilty to the charges against him, but was found incompetent to stand trial last week.

Siders and her husband have been ordered to have no contact.

On Wednesday, a judge deemed Elizabeth Siders a flight risk and raised her bail from $250,000 to $550,000.

FLORIDA AG SEEKS DEATH PENALTY FOR COUPLE WHO ALLEGEDLY HELD 4 CHILDREN IN ‘ROLLING PRISON’ FOR NEARLY 7 YEARS

In July, investigators found the children — ranging in age from 17 months to 18 years old — living in deplorable conditions inside a home in Hamden.

They were initially investigating child sexual abuse allegations regarding Siders's extended family members: Brandon Henderson, the longtime partner of Gary Siders Jr.’s sister, and Joshua Saunders, a cousin of the 16 rescued children, the FOX 8 report states.

item.title: Unearthed clip exposes what 'DEI Queen' in razor-thin House race thought of 'Back the Blue' law
item.description: Christina Bohannan called Iowa's "back the blue" law an "overreaction" to the George Floyd riots, fueling fresh Republican soft-on-crime attacks.
item.content:encoded:
Christina Bohannan, an Iowa state legislator and the Democratic nominee in one of the country’s most competitive districts, once opposed an Iowa "Back the Blue" law passed in the wake of the 2020 George Floyd riots, calling it an "overreaction."

"I think that we’re seeing a backlash and, frankly, an exaggerated backlash, an overreaction to all of that," Bohannan said at a 2021 virtual legislative forumon social justice issues.

"That’s what’s happening. A lot of this is happening because they just don’t have a lot of minorities in their districts, they don’t interact with people on any kind of regular basis and so they don’t see these issues."

To some onlooking critics, her resurfaced comments are further proof of what they’ve characterized as her soft-on-crime stances — positions they believe are at odds with the electorate of the Hawkeye State as she wages her third campaign to unseat Rep. Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa.

WATCH: BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT CALLED IOWA A 'BACKWATER' OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES BAN

"Christina Bohannan achieved the ultra-rare-final-boss level of woke where police are bad, criminals are good, and anyone who disagrees is racist," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"There is a reason why this DEI Queen has been rejected twice by voters - she is straight up nuts, and her soft-on-crime agenda would endanger all Iowans."

Bohannan launched her career in education, teaching at the University of Iowa College of Law, where she remained until, in 2020, she won a seat in the Iowa House of Representatives, unseating a 20-year Democratic incumbent.

Bohannan has run for Congress before.

In 2022, she lost to Miller-Meeks in a 53.4% to 46.6% contest. She tried again in 2024 and got closer, losing by a fraction of a percent: 50.0% to 49.8% — just 799 votes.

VANCE, CRUZ, HEAD TO IOWA ON 2026 MISSIONS AS 2028 GOP RACE TO SUCCEED TRUMP HEATS UP

In all three races, Republicans have attacked her on her statements as an academic and her voting record as a state legislator, painting her as a soft-on-crime candidate.

In the resurfaced clip, Bohannan was referring to Senate File 342, signed by Gov. Kim Reynolds in 2021. Among other provisions, the bill raised penalties for rioting, making it a class D felony punishable by five years behind bars, and implemented more stringent punishments for unlawful assembly.

The law came amid a wave of anti-police sentiment that swept the country after George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, died after then-officer Derek Chauvin knelt on his neck area during a restraint. The incident sparked widespread debate on law enforcement safety and profiling. Where states like Minnesota and Washington passed restrictions on police and other law enforcement officers, Iowa lawmakers rallied to their support.

Iowa Rep. Jarad Klein, a Republican and the bill’s sponsor, framed the legislation as a clear way to support embattled public servants in a floor speech.

"Let me be clear: If you support law enforcement, truly support law enforcement, you will be voting ‘yes’ tonight. If you stand up and say you support law enforcement, your words will become meaningless with a ‘no’ vote. Actions speak louder than words," Klein said.

Gov. Reynolds echoed that thinking at her signing.

"I made it clear in my Condition of the State Address that Iowa’s law enforcement will always have my respect, and I will always have their back. Today’s bill embodies that commitment in a historic way. The public peace is too important, and the safety of our officers too precious, to tolerate destructive behavior," Reynolds said in a press release.

For her own part, Bohannan said she opposed the legislation, arguing it went too far.

"The bill that’s coming over to the House from the Senate about the protestors actually would make it okay for a person to drive negligently or grossly negligently and hit a protestor and there would be immunity for that. It’s sick. These are kids, mostly," she said.

UNEARTHED CLIP EXPOSES MORE ANTI-POLICE RHETORIC AS EL-SAYED GETS GRILLED FOR DELETING SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

The final version of the bill does have a provision that protects drivers from civil liability. But it only applies to drivers "exercising due care" and who cause injury to someone engaging in disorderly conduct by blocking traffic in a public street or highway.

Bohannan’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital on her statements from 2021 or whether she stood by her views of the "Back the Blue" bill.

item.title: House GOP lawmaker under fire by fellow Republicans after ad bashing Trump on immigration
item.description: Rep. María Elvira Salazar's ad told President Donald Trump his immigration enforcement has gone too far, drawing sharp rebukes from the Freedom Caucus.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A House GOP lawmaker’s pointed message to President Donald Trump criticizing his immigration policy is under fire from her Republican colleagues.

Rep. María Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., released a campaign ad on Thursday that attacked Trump’s handling of immigration enforcement, specifically arguing that he has gone too far in pursuing people without criminal records.

"President Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts should be applauded and continue as is," House Freedom Caucus leaders said in an official statement first shared with Fox News Digital.

"Any alien who enters this country illegally has committed a crime. The United States should deport every illegal alien. This is America, and this government should be ensuring the dignity of American citizens. Illegal aliens can enjoy dignity in their home country or come to this country legally."

GOP INFIGHTING ERUPTS OVER IMMIGRATION BILL THAT WOULD SHIELD MILLIONS FROM DEPORTATION

The statement continued, "Granting illegal aliens any legal status to remain in the United States is amnesty. We reject amnesty. The House Freedom Caucus stands with President Trump: secure the border, enforce the law, and lock these policies into statute, so no future administration can erase them with a pen."

TRUMP DHS CHIEF UNDER FIRE FROM CONSERVATIVES AFTER IMMIGRATION SPEECH IGNITES BACKLASH

The ad takes place outside the White House, with Salazar directly addressing the camera.
"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,"
Salazar said. "Be careful what your advisors are telling you about immigration policy. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

"You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land. And only you can do that," she said.

TRUMP-BACKED REPUBLICAN SURVIVES PRIMARY AFTER BUCKING HIM ON DEPORTATIONS

It’s a notable choice of words, given that her district voted for Trump by double digits in 2024. But she’s one of several Hispanic lawmakers in the House GOP who have been warning their party could be alienating Hispanic and Latino voters who were critical to Republican wins in recent years.

Salazar’s South Florida district is currently rated R+6 by the nonpartisan Cook political report, meaning it’s likely to stay in Republican hands. But Democrats are targeting her seat as a potential pickup opportunity as they work to win back control of the House.

She previously took heat from the Freedom Caucus over her bipartisan legislation to reform the asylum process and give a legal pathway to undocumented people already in the U.S. who have not committed crimes.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also pushed back on Salazar, telling Fox News in a statement: "DHS is focused on delivering the most HISTORIC mass deportation campaign in American history—exactly as President Trump promised."

"Whether Congresswoman Salazar likes it or not, the men and women of ICE are enforcing the laws passed by Congress. To be clear: the only thing America should be giving illegal aliens is a one-way ticket home, or a generous $3,000 check for them to self-deport immediately. We will not ignore the rule of law," the DHS spokesperson said.

item.title: 'Gone too far:' GOP candidate runs to Trump’s left on signature issue in deep red district
item.description: Maria Elvira Salazar tells Trump his immigration enforcement has gone too far, warning that Hispanics who backed him in 2024 now feel betrayed.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Republican who represents a solidly red district in Miami, has broken with the president on immigration as the midterms cycle hits a fever pitch.

"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar said in a newly released campaign advertisement. "Be careful what your advisors are telling you about immigration policy. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today. You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism."

"I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land," she continued.

THE HISPANIC VOTE IS UP FOR GRABS IN 2026. CANDIDATES WHO IGNORE IT WILL LOSE

A Fox News poll released Wednesday found President Donald Trump’s overall approval rating at 39%, with 61% of registered voters disapproving of his job performance.

Voters disapprove of Trump generally by a margin of 61% to 39%, according to the poll. On immigration, however, only 56% of voters are unhappy with the president's performance, beating out his handling of the economy and foreign policy.

VOTERS SAY REPUBLICANS OUTDO DEMOCRATS ON THESE KEY ISSUES: FOX NEWS POLL

Salazar’s break with the president on immigration follows a legislative record that has combined tougher enforcement measures with support for legal-status reforms.

During her time in Congress, Salazar has supported tougher border enforcement while also backing legislation that would provide legal status to some long-term noncitizens, including through the bipartisan DIGNITY Act.

She also voted for the 2023 Secure the Border Act and the 2025 Laken Riley Act, which expanded immigration enforcement and required the detention of certain undocumented immigrants accused of crimes.

TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94%

Trump’s hardline stance on immigration, likewise, is nothing new.

The issue defined his initial rise to power during the 2016 presidential election, and he leaned heavily into promises of deportations while on the campaign trail in 2024. Amid the president’s hawkish rhetoric, Hispanics in places such as the Miami metropolitan area and along the Southern border shifted heavily to the right.

Trump has endorsed Salazar’s bid for reelection.

The Salazar campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

item.title: The New Yorker claims women can be 'kind of pregnant' in article questioning pregnancy tests
item.description: The New Yorker faced backlash for promoting an essay claiming a woman could be "kind of pregnant," sparking debate over pregnancy as a biological state.
item.content:encoded:
The New Yorker drew criticism Thursday after promoting an essay that described the binary distinction between being pregnant and not pregnant as "misleading" and said a woman could be "kind of pregnant" or "a little bit pregnant."

The essay, "The Unsettling Ambiguity of Early Pregnancy," by Apoorva Tadepalli, examined the uncertainty surrounding early pregnancy tests, miscarriage and viability through the writer's experience with multiple pregnancy losses and her current pregnancy. 

The magazine promoted the piece on X by saying at-home tests capture only a moment when an embryo has implanted and that someone could be "kind of pregnant, a little bit pregnant, or almost pregnant, or maybe pregnant" while still testing positive.

MED SCHOOL DEANS COME UP EMPTY IN TENSE HEARING WHEN ASKED POINT BLANK IF MEN CAN HAVE BABIES: 'RIDICULOUS'

Los Angeles County Republican Party Chair Roxanne Hoge, a mother of four, told Fox News Digital that uncertainty over whether a pregnancy will remain viable does not change whether a woman is pregnant.

"As a mother of four and an actual biological woman, I must applaud the author for noticing that women do, in fact, make babies," she said. "While I sympathize with her on the very sad reality of carrying a pregnancy after a loss, this was a lot of words to try and pretend that a fetus is a clump of cells. You're either pregnant or you're not."

Elizabeth Barcohana, America First Policy Institute California ambassador to the America First Women's initiative, said the distinction should be between the existence of a pregnancy and whether a woman knows that pregnancy is viable.

"A woman cannot be ‘a little bit pregnant.’ Pregnancy is a physical, biological state that begins when a fertilized embryo implants in the uterus and triggers a chemical hormonal reaction," Barcohana said Thursday in a statement to Fox News Digital. "This article is not about being pregnant. It is about a woman’s experience about knowing whether she is carrying a viable healthy pregnancy."

Tadepalli described testing positive during five pregnancies and spending periods of those pregnancies unsure whether she would miscarry. She said those experiences affected her ability to emotionally embrace her current pregnancy, with much of the essay examining what early testing can and cannot tell women about what will happen next.

PRO-LIFE PUBLISHER FACING DEMANDS TO RETRACT CALLING ABORTION ‘KILLING’ FIRES BACK: ‘THE ANSWER IS NO’

Lisa Cusack, president of the Don’t L.A. My Burbank PAC, told Fox News Digital she viewed the article’s framing as an attempt to make pregnancy more subjective while arguing that uncertainty in early testing does not change whether a woman is pregnant.

"This article just seems like a tortured attempt to make pregnancy into a subject experience in order to justify abortion," she said. "The fact that an at-home pregnancy isn’t sophisticated enough to pick up the beginning stages of every pregnancy doesn’t mean you’re ‘kind of pregnant,’ or that pregnancy itself, which literally begins with conception and ends with birth, is ‘nonlinear.’

"Women have always known that early pregnancies sometimes don’t take or show up on tests, but that doesn’t change the fact that you’re either pregnant or not, whether you know it or not or want it or not."

WHAT MY SON'S ULTRASOUND TAUGHT ME ABOUT ABORTION — AND MASSACHUSETTS IGNORES

Barcohana said that element of the essay was relatable to women who have experienced pregnancy loss and blamed The New Yorker’s presentation for shifting attention away from it.

"The New Yorker’s editors betrayed the author with this provocative headline, because what she’s really talking about — in a vulnerable way that millions of women can empathize with — is the utility and impact on women of unreliable early testing," she said. "She tried to talk about something totally legitimate for women trying to start a family, and they [editors] hijacked it."

Fox News Digital reached out to The New Yorker for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

The distinction between detecting pregnancy and determining whether it is viable is also reflected in medical guidance. The Food and Drug Administration says at-home pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, a hormone produced after a fertilized egg is attached to the uterine wall. The agency notes that testing too early can produce inaccurate results and that a positive home test does not provide information about how a pregnancy will develop.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists states that pregnancy begins when a fertilized egg is implanted in the uterus, while pregnancy viability can require additional evaluation as development progresses.

item.title: Meyer Lansky’s grandson reflects on late mobster's crime empire, Las Vegas legacy and missing millions
item.description: Meyer Lansky II reveals personal letters and memories of his mob boss grandfather in a new book exploring the infamous organized crime figure's legacy.
item.content:encoded:
To Prohibition-era gangsters, history buffs and true crime aficionados, he was Meyer Lansky, the financial mastermind who built an international gambling empire. To his namesake, he was simply "grandpa."

Meyer Lansky II, the grandson of the late mob boss who helped establish organized crime across the nation, reflects on his grandfather through personal letters, photographs and firsthand memories in his new book with S. J. Peddie, "The Lansky Legacy: The Life and Letters of Meyer Lansky."

"He never mentioned the names of anybody that he worked with. He was always cautious with that," Lansky told Fox News Digital.

CHARLES MANSON'S GRANDDAUGHTER REVEALS MOMENT SHE DISCOVERED DARK FAMILY SECRET: 'IT WAS DEVASTATING'

Growing up in Washington state, the younger Lansky initially saw his grandfather as a stern, serious figure who strictly compartmentalized his life. The elder Lansky never brought up his underworld dealings; instead, he focused on teaching his grandson how to present himself to the world, introducing him to fine details like tie pins and shoehorns.

"Growing up in Washington state, I wasn't exposed to those kinds of things anywhere else," Lansky said. "He was always asking me about my grades, my studies and what books I was reading.

"He’d give me basic advice: ‘Whatever you do, do a good job. Be honest with people, provide good service and people will come back to you.’"

SAMMY 'THE BULL' REVEALS WHY HIS LOVE FOR JOHN GOTTI TURNED INTO PRISON HATE

The elder Lansky, widely dubbed the "mob's accountant," rose to prominence in the early 20th century alongside childhood friends Benjamin "Bugsy" Siegel and Charles "Lucky" Luciano. Together, they revolutionized organized crime, building lucrative gambling operations from Havana to Las Vegas.

"He was right alongside Luciano and Bugsy Siegel during the transformation of the syndicate into the modern American Mafia," Lansky said.

That reputation carried real-world danger. The younger Lansky recalled a chilling incident from his childhood, when his grandfather's notoriety and perceived wealth nearly led to his kidnapping.

As he grew older, the veil began to slip.

EX-MOB CAPO ALLEGES FURIOUS RFK WEAPONIZED THE FBI AGAINST HIS FATHER OVER MARILYN MONROE

"One day I was listening to the radio and heard that Treasury Secretary John Connally was going to Las Vegas to investigate Meyer Lansky," he said, referencing the decades-long, unsuccessful federal effort to convict his grandfather.

"When my grandfather visited a week later, I told him, ‘Hey, I heard your name on the radio.’ He looked at me, smiled, and said, ‘You did?’ He didn't elaborate, but I knew at that point he realized I was going to figure out who he really was."

EX-COLOMBO CRIME FAMILY CAPO REVEALS HOW GAS TAX SCHEME RAKED IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS WEEKLY

While mob historians contend that the Polish-born gangster perfected modern money laundering and amassed vast fortunes, a central mystery remains: What happened to the money?

If the elder Lansky stashed away millions, his grandson noted, the family never saw it.

Yet, the physical legacy remains impossible to ignore.

REDDIT DEBATE REVEALS LAS VEGAS HAS BECOME FAR MORE THAN A GAMBLING DESTINATION FOR MILLIONS OF VISITORS

"He was heavily involved in transforming the American Mafia into something that still holds an irresistible, nostalgic grip on culture," Lansky said. "These guys are major figures of history.

"They took a barren desert and turned it into a sophisticated gambling empire."

item.title: Two regular dudes are about to fish for $1.25 million against the best bass anglers in the world
item.description: Eric Giessing and Kyle Carr will fish against 60 elite pros including Jacob Wheeler for a record $3.25 million purse on Old Hickory Lake this fall.
item.content:encoded:
Eric Giessing and Kyle Carr are about to find out exactly how good they are at bass fishing.

World Bass Enterprises (WBE) announced this week that Giessing, a 53-year-old amateur angler from Farmington, Mo., and Carr, a 39-year-old local tournament fisherman from Gatesville, Texas, have been selected as the two "Average Joes" who will compete in The Champions this fall.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

And WBE isn't sticking them in some separate amateur division. They're fishing the same tournament, for the same money, against 60 of the best professional bass anglers in the world.

That includes a $3.25 million purse and $1.25 million for the winner. That’s the largest purse in bass fishing history.

"Fans of every sport wonder how they'd fare competing against the pros," WBE founder and CEO Brian Bird said. "We thought it would be neat to give bass fishing fans the chance to actually answer that question. Eric and Kyle will now get to see how they stack up against the pros."

Well, they're certainly going to get an answer.

When Bird first told OutKick OutDoors about the Average Joes concept earlier this summer, the two spots were still up for grabs.

Now we know the contestants, and WBE has since revealed the professional field they'll have to deal with.

The Champions will pit its Stars and Stripes rosters against one another, bringing together elite anglers from the Bassmaster and Major League Fishing worlds.

And there aren't many soft spots on either side.

Start with Trey McKinney, whom OutKick OutDoors spoke with earlier this month after he wrapped up a historic Bassmaster Elite season. The 21-year-old became the youngest Bassmaster Angler of the Year in history and, at the St. Lawrence River finale, also broke the B.A.S.S. record for the heaviest one-day bag of smallmouth bass.

Then there is Jordan Lee, a two-time Bassmaster Classic champion who won the sport's marquee event in consecutive years in 2017 and 2018. Hank Cherry is also a back-to-back Classic champion, while Jason Christie won the 2022 Classic.

TREY MCKINNEY SAYS BASSMASTER VETERANS MADE HIM EARN THEIR RESPECT BEFORE HISTORY AOY SEASON

And that's just one side of the field.

The Stripes roster includes Jacob Wheeler, who has won four Bass Pro Tour Angler of the Year titles and captured REDCREST in 2026. Wheeler has racked up 12 Bass Pro Tour wins since the circuit began in 2019.

There's also Dustin Connell, the only three-time REDCREST champion, and reigning 2026 Bass Pro Tour Angler of the Year Zack Birge.

Oh, and Ott DeFoe, who won the 2019 Bassmaster Classic in Knoxville, is in there too.

So, yeah. Good luck, fellas.

To be fair to Giessing and Carr, "Average Joe" doesn't mean either guy wandered into Bass Pro Shops last week and bought his first rod.

Both have tournament experience.

Giessing has been an amateur angler for five years and fishes primarily around Lake of the Ozarks. He started fishing as a kid with his late father and has competed in a variety of amateur events in recent years.

And he's not shy about wanting to see how far he can take it.

"My goal is to continue growing as a competitor, learning from every experience, and pushing myself to see how far I can take this passion," Giessing said. "I consider myself a power fisherman and enjoy the challenge of finding aggressive fish and figuring out what it takes to get them in the boat."

Giessing said his ultimate goal would be reaching the professional ranks and competing at the highest level of tournament bass fishing.

Well, this should be one hell of an audition.

Carr also grew up fishing with his dad and now competes with Cen-Tex Bass Hunters in Belton, Texas, as well as the Tuesday Night Tight Lines 3x9 Series on Stillhouse Hollow Lake.

"My dad taught me from an early age what it means to be a sportsman, respect the outdoors, and appreciate conservation," Carr said. "I've been hooked on bass fishing since I was a kid, and these days I enjoy putting that passion to work."

He added: "At the end of the day, I just enjoy being on the water, chasing bass, and competing with good people who share the same passion for fishing."

The jump from a Tuesday night tournament to lining up against Wheeler, McKinney, Connell and a pile of Bassmaster Classic champions is admittedly a pretty significant one.

But that's also what makes this interesting.

The inaugural Champions tournament will take place Oct. 28-Nov. 1 on Old Hickory Lake at Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tenn., just outside Nashville.

The concept from the beginning has been to put top anglers from the sport's major professional circuits on the same water and settle things in one big-money event.

Bird said Giessing and Carr won't be treated any differently just because they got into the field through a sweepstakes.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

"We're going to roll out the red carpet for them and treat them the same way we treat the pro anglers," Bird said. "Both 'Average Joes' have a chance to win the grand prize and the ultimate bragging rights, but no matter what, they'll be leaving Nashville with some prize money and a great story to tell."

item.title: NFL's highest-paid TE George Kittle reveals favorite purchase: A 50-foot flagpole for a massive American flag
item.description: George Kittle revealed his favorite splurge purchase is a 50-foot American flagpole next to the football field on his 178-acre Tennessee ranch.
item.content:encoded:
George Kittle signed the richest contract for a tight end in NFL history in April 2025, but it was also his third major deal. By the time the final contract expires in 2029, the three deals will have paid him approximately $155 million.

So the obvious question many athletes often hear was asked by the guys from the "Bussin' With the Boys" podcast: What is Kittle’s favorite splurge purchase of all time?

"Building a football field at my house, building a workout facility, putting up a 50-foot American flagpole," Kittle said. "That's probably my favorite purchase on my property I've made. My wife really likes that one."

THE STORY BEHIND BETSY ROSS AND THE FIRST AMERICAN FLAG AS AMERICA CELEBRATES 250TH BIRTHDAY

The 50-foot American flagpole now sits on Kittle's offseason home, which is a roughly 178-acre ranch in the Nashville area of Tennessee.

And, of course, the 50-foot flagpole, as tall as a typical four- or five-story building, displays one enormous flag.

"It's pretty f-----g massive," Kittle said. "Right when you pull in, it sits right next to the football field. It's the only thing you can f-----g see."

The sight of Old Glory — and all it represents — waving in the wind has got to fire Kittle up.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"It does," he said. "I saw it last night. We have lights pointing up at it, and I was just, had just got out of the car, I was like, 'Oh, God, it's so beautiful.'

"So, yeah, that's one of my favorite purchases."

Look, the NFL gets a lot of bad publicity sometimes for the problems some of its employees have with domestic abuse or driving under the influence.

The league itself has been ripped by conservatives for posting social justice messaging on its fields, and it has been accused of taking advantage of its antitrust exemption under the 1961 Sports Broadcasting Act.

But this serves as a reminder that the league is made up of plenty of people like Kittle.

They're people who love America. They're proud Americans.

They are patriots, really.

No, not every one of those is erecting a 50-foot flagpole. But so far this year, at least, none are kneeling when the flag is the center of attention during the national anthem.

George Kittle is one of the good guys.

item.title: Radical El-Sayed ally doubles down on anti-American rhetoric with stunning terrorist comparison
item.description: Hasan Piker told Axios that America is worse than al-Qaeda "pound for pound," deepening scrutiny of his ties to Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate race.
item.content:encoded:
A popular far-left streamer tied the Democratic nominee in the high-stakes U.S. Senate race in Michigan doubled down on anti-American comments he's made in the past during an on-camera interview released Thursday.

Hasan Piker was featured in an episode of "The Axios Show" taped in Los Angeles, where he resides, where interviewer Alex Thompson recalled the internet personality's past claim that "America is the top dog in terrorism."

"Do you think America, then, is worse than al-Qaeda?" Thomspon asked.

HASAN PIKER INSISTS ABDUL EL-SAYED ASKED HIM TO 'STUMP' FOR MICHIGAN CAMPAIGN AMID BACKLASH

"Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes," Piker replied. "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world."

"I think that that is not only terror that we are waging on regular civilians, and nations in the periphery, but it's also having consequences on ourselves," the Twitch streamer continued. "It's having dramatic consequences on the home front."

"One clear example of this is what we did in Minab [Iran],' Piker said, referring to American attacks earlier this year that struck a school. A United Nations mission said it found "reasonable grounds" to believe that the U.S. committed a war crime. "There's no distinction between blowing up a school, tripple-tapping it with Tomahawk missiles. If you're killing 140 school girls, that is an act of terror."

Piker conceded that not all Americans are terrorists, but still called for an "environment of accountability."

EL-SAYED PALS AROUND WITH FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER THE DAY BEFORE CRUCIAL MICHIGAN SENATE ELECTION

Piker is closely tied to Abdul El-Sayed, the controversial far-left U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan. Piker joined El-Sayed on the campaign trail during primary season. The two were pictured partying together on the night El-Sayed ended up winning his primary election.

Since winning the Democratic primary, El-Sayed hasn't been able to shake Piker's shadow, and has refused to condemn him for past controversial comments. Instead the candidate has painting him as a "streamer from California" who has no bearing on the race in Michigan in attempts to distance himself from Piker's more radical views and comments.

Piker said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11." He has also praised Mao Zedong and Communist China, said capitalists should be murdered in the streets and is known for making antisemitic comments.

El-Sayed's campaign responded to Piker's comments on The Axios Show, but did not mention Piker by name.

ABDUL EL-SAYED DISMISSES QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER TIES ON 'FACE THE NATION,' PIVOTS TO GROCERIES

"I do not agree with this statement [on al-Qaeda], nor do I give much weight to the statements made by a social media streamer," the campaign told Axios. "I am more concerned with the dangerous policies of Donald Trump and Mike Rogers that are raising the prices of gas, groceries and healthcare for Michiganders."

El-Sayed's campaign reiterated that statement when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

During a trip to Washington, D.C. on Wednesday to meet with potential future colleagues, El-Sayed was caught on camera walking into the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC). When asked by Fox News Digital whether he would condemn Piker, El-Sayed waved off the question and swiftly ducked into the building where he sat down with Democrat senators.

El-Sayed's staff later banned Fox News Digital from joining an impromptu post-meeting press event where he took questions and discussed a range of issues key to the 2026 midterms.

item.title: Fox News Poll: 71% think Trump administration lacks plan to end Iran war
item.description: A Fox News poll finds 70% of voters say Trump lacks a clear strategy for the Iran war, while 60% now call the military action the wrong decision.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly seven months into the war with Iran, a new Fox News national survey finds views souring as voters feel the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the war, a growing number think the conflict will make the U.S. less safe and a majority believes the decision to take military action was wrong.

Seven in 10 voters think the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the conflict, including 95% of Democrats, 83% of independents and 43% of Republicans.

In addition, a growing 47% of voters say the conflict will make the U.S. less safe in the long run, up from 39% in April. By comparison, 32% think it will make the country safer, and 20% say there will be no difference. The rise in concern is largest among White voters, voters under 45 and independents.

Sixty percent say U.S. military action against Iran was the wrong decision, while 37% say it was right, widening the margin to 23 points, up from 17 points in June (58% to 41%). Attitudes against the war have increased modestly across most demographic groups, with the largest shifts among Hispanic voters, voters under age 30, moderates and voters 65 and over.

FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE

"Typically, the public rallies around the president in response to a foreign policy crisis," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "But two things are different here. First, President Trump hasn’t consistently and forcefully made the case for the war, and the U.S. doesn’t have boots on the ground. Both of those things matter for public opinion."

FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

Trump’s overall job performance stands at 39% approval and 61% disapproval.

The president’s ratings on foreign policy are underwater by 24 points. His 37% approval is a second-term low and is just one point above his first-term low of 36% in September 2019.

When asked to name the most important issue facing the country, in their own words, only 4% of voters say Iran and a miniscule 1% name foreign policy in general. By comparison, 34% mention the top issue of the cost of living.

Meanwhile, by a 10-point margin, more voters say the Democrats are better equipped to handle foreign policy than the Republicans, a reversal from the previous midterm cycle when Republicans were more trusted by 6 points in September 2022.

Israel and Ukraine

A low of 48% say they side more with the Israelis than the Palestinians (38%) in the ongoing conflict in Gaza. That is down from 54% in June and a high of 68% at the conflict’s outset in October 2023.

Since 2023, the sharpest decline in support for Israel — down at least 20 points — comes from women, Hispanic voters, voters under age 45, voters with a college degree and Democrats. Republican support has fallen 10 points during the same time.

On Ukraine, voters favor the U.S. continuing to provide financial aid to fight Russia by 16 points (55% to 39%), roughly unchanged during the past two years. Democrats favor supporting Ukraine, while Republicans and independents are divided.

One more thing…

Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s upcoming visit to the U.S., more than twice as many voters say Trump is not tough enough on China (45%) as say he is too tough (20%). Three in 10 (30%) say his approach is about right.

There is bipartisan agreement on this: the largest share of Democrats (44%), Republicans (47%), and independents (44%) say Trump is not tough enough on China.  Republicans are more split, with 43% saying his approach is about right.

Conducted September 11-14, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,211 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (96) and cellphones (821) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (294). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. 

Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. item.title: Fox News Poll: Majority says immigration enforcement has crossed the line
item.description: A Fox News poll finds Trump's immigration approval at 43%, and 53% of voters say ICE enforcement has gone too far, nearly erasing the GOP's edge.
item.content:encoded:
A 53% majority of registered voters say the Trump administration’s enforcement of immigration laws has gone too far, according to new Fox News polling, a view that has stayed consistent since June 2025. 

The remaining voters are split between enforcement not going far enough and enforcement that's just about right (23% each).

The results skew along party lines: 87% of Democrats and 60% of independents say enforcement has gone too far, while most Republicans split between not far enough (40%) and about right (43%).

Among those saying enforcement has gone too far, voters are divided on the reason: 45% point to the government using too much force, while 49% say the wrong people are being targeted.

Democrats say the government is targeting the wrong people (by 7 points) while independents say it’s because of using too much force (by 2 points). There are not enough Republicans saying the enforcement has gone too far to draw meaningful conclusions.

Consequently, President Trump’s approval rating on immigration sits at 43%, down from a high of 48% last summer.

For the past four years, until this summer, voters consistently said the Republicans would do a better job handling immigration than the Democrats. That advantage has all but disappeared, as voters are split between the parties (48% D vs. 49% R). The Democrats are competitive on immigration due to independents backing them over the GOP by 6 points and 15% of non-MAGA Republicans preferring the Democrats.

FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS

"The immigration issue has been defined in terms of border security since the Biden years," says Daron Shaw, the GOP pollster who helps conduct the survey with Democrat Chris Anderson. "But voters now think of immigration policy as ICE crackdowns, and many say these have been too aggressive."

Despite fewer than 1 in 10 (8%) voters identifying immigration as their priority, it only trails the cost of living (34%) and the broader economy (14%) as the most important issue facing the country.

One more thing…

Nearly two-thirds of voters (63%) agree that a child born to an illegal immigrant in the United States should automatically become a citizen. While overall support has softened from previous highs around 67-69%, it’s still far above its low of 45% in 2006.

Among Hispanic voters, two-thirds disapprove of Trump’s overall job performance and his handling of immigration. They trust the Democrats over the Republicans on the issue by 19 points, while 60% say immigration enforcement has gone too far.

Three-quarters of Hispanic voters think citizenship should be guaranteed for those born in the U.S. to illegal immigrant parents.

item.title: Costco's unexpected new role in Americans' love lives: 'Secret sauce is the sampling'
item.description: From "Camp Costco" veterans meetups to food court date nights, the warehouse club is where Americans are building unexpected social connections.
item.content:encoded:
As more of life moves online, people are finding an in-person connection somewhere unexpected: the aisles and food court of their local Costco.

The membership warehouse club, known for its bulk grocery items and huge packs of home supplies, has joined the likes of bars, churches and parks as a public spot where people socialize, make friends and may spark or renew romance.

Costco has become what sociologists call a "third place," a communal gathering spot where people build community outside their home and work environments, USA Today reported.

GROCERY STORE SWITCH COULD SAVE AMERICANS MONEY WHILE SHAKING UP DINNER ROUTINES

"Costco has turned shopping into an experience, not just an errand," Phil Lempert, a consumer and trend analyst known as the "SupermarketGuru," told Fox News Digital. "You go in for paper towels and walk out having sampled food, discovered something unexpected and maybe bumped into someone you know. Their secret sauce is the sampling."

University of California, Davis students Sharon Hwang, Katrina Le and Steven Zhang organize a group of fellow students for a trip to their local Costco for a food court meal once or twice a quarter, USA Today reported.

"If something small like a Costco trip can help someone meet new friends or feel a little bit connected, then I feel like we accomplished something," Hwang told the publication.

Friends and social media influencers Analyse Talavera and Carmen Rene Smith have traded costly dinner catchups for Costco errand runs.

"Especially in this economy, instead of going out and dropping $200 on dinner — which Analyse and I are good for — we go to Costco and stock up on meal prep for the week and then top it off with a $3 fro yo," Smith told USA Today.

More than 25 years after two military veterans began meeting at their neighborhood Costco in Brentwood, Tennessee, for a Friday hot dog, the Middle Tennessee Veterans Support Group — "Camp Costco" — is still going strong, now supporting a couple of hundred service members across generations.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Nobody cares what rank you were or what service you were in," Marine veteran and group member Paul Napoli told USA Today. "Everybody mixes together."

Some couples use their shopping trips as a substitute for date night, dubbing it "clubbing for married folks" or "the Kirkland Signature date night" after Costco's in-house brand.

Still others use the store to find love, and some couples have chosen Costco as the venue for their nuptials, according to Reddit posts.

It can also be a fun place to explore, Lempert said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Costco creates a kind of retail ritual: the treasure hunt, the samples, the food court, the great deal you want to tell somebody about," he said. "Consumers aren't just buying products. They're sharing an experience, and that's incredibly powerful in an increasingly digital and isolated shopping world."

The appetite for that experience comes as in-person connection erodes elsewhere. Americans now spend about 35 minutes a day socializing, down from 45 minutes 20 years ago, and only 30% do any face-to-face socializing on a given day, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' American Time Use Survey.

The surgeon general's 2023 advisory found roughly half of adults experience loneliness, and the Survey Center on American Life reports 44% have nowhere in their community to go regularly.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Costco shoppers, by contrast, are loyal, averaging 31 trips to the warehouse annually, according to consumer analytics firm Numerator.

They also make the food court a regular habit, spending in line with what they spend at major regional fast-food chains, including In-N-Out.

The membership model further creates a social aspect and sense of belonging, Lempert said.

"Membership changes the psychology of shopping — it makes one feel special," he said. "You’re not simply a customer walking into a store; you're a member of a club. Costco has essentially made the membership card part of the consumer's identity."

BILL BELICHICK'S SON RESIGNS AS NORTH CAROLINA'S DEFENSIVE COORDINATOR AS INVESTIGATION INTO CULTURE CLOSES

Jordon is not the GM. She's not handling everything for him day to day. She's copied on a few emails and helping out with scheduling unrelated to UNC. Furthermore, she's been lying low recently.

item.title: Mamdani's new $4M NYC public bathrooms auto-open doors after 10 minutes
item.description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's $4 million public bathroom pilot installs Throne Labs units across NYC, but a strict 10-minute limit ends with the door opening.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani rolled out a $4 million public bathroom pilot Wednesday in Queens that will install 17 Throne Labs units across all five boroughs to address the city's restroom shortage. 

Company co-founder and COO Jessica Heinzelman explained that users get 10 minutes before escalating warnings culminate in the door automatically opening.

Heinzelman detailed the final warning during a city news conference, saying users receive flashing lights and an audio notification before the door opens.

SMART TOILET SEAT COULD DETECT AFIB IN 30 SECONDS

"At 10 minutes, there are flashing lights. The audio comes on. And this is both in English and Spanish for all of these indicators," she said. 

"It says, ‘The door — your time is up, the door is opening.’ The door’s opening. That extends for about 30 seconds. So, if you are still pants down, we're not going to open the door on you. But then the door does open."

Heinzelman told Fox News Digital Thursday that Throne Labs settled on the 10-minute restriction after reviewing typical public restroom limits and measuring how long people actually spend inside its units, saying most users leave well before the deadline.

"The 10-min limit is a common standard for most timed public restrooms. We further validated measuring the average throne use time, with the vast majority of users across our markets leaving within 3½ minutes," she said. "Users are notified of the time limit prior to entering, and the throne provides multiple audio and visual warnings throughout the use.

"At the tail-end of the use there is 30 seconds of audio and visual queues [sic] to leave. This has proven successful in other cities, balancing human needs and mitigating loitering."

MAMDANI LAUNCHES FAST-TRACK HOUSING-COURT PUSH, SAYS LANDLORDS UNABLE TO COMPLY ‘SHOULD NOT BE A LANDLORD’

Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg told Fox News Digital Thursday that the unusual feature should be weighed against New York City's longstanding shortage of public bathrooms and the high cost of building traditional facilities.

"Anyone who’s walked the streets of New York knows the lack of basic public facilities is a real quality-of-life problem," he said. "Cities have managed to spend extraordinary sums building individual public toilets, so if this modular pilot can actually get clean, safe bathrooms on the street for a fraction of that, it’s a victory for municipal common sense.

"After all, I’d much rather see the mayor doing the gritty, unglamorous work of solving an actual New York City problem than spending his time grandstanding about Middle East policy."

AOC SLAMS ‘OPPRESSED’ TRUMP STATES WHILE TOUTING NYC SERVICES DESPITE $5B DEFICIT AND TRANSIT CRIME SPIKE

The one-year pilot will place the ADA-accessible units at high-traffic locations in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island. According to the Mayor's Office, they will be free, operate daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. and can be opened through text message, QR code, the Throne app or physical tap cards distributed through community partners.

Mamdani said the modular approach allows the city to avoid some of the infrastructure expenses associated with permanent bathrooms because the units do not require direct connections to water, sewer or power systems. During the news conference, he compared the price of the entire pilot with the historical cost of a single city restroom.

"Seventeen costs about what one public restroom has historically cost in New York City. And that is part of why we have not built that many, because we've seen the cost of these restrooms just escalate year after year," Mamdani said.

The 10-minute limit is designed partly to deter loitering and extended occupation. Throne Labs says users receive reminders at five and eight minutes, flashing lights and a more urgent message at 10 minutes and the door opens at 10 minutes and 30 seconds. The company said 81% of users across its network finish within five minutes and more than 95% at one downtown Los Angeles location finish within 10 minutes.

NIGHTTIME BATHROOM TRIPS COULD REVEAL HIDDEN HEALTH ISSUES — HERE'S WHEN TO WORRY

The same technology is already being used in California. Caltrain's current restroom pilot uses Throne units at Redwood City, Sunnyvale and Palo Alto stations and tells riders that after the 10-minute limit, "a visual and auditory warning will sound before the doors are opened."

Long Beach also launched four Throne units in 2025 and subsequently extended its partnership after the initial pilot. The city's original announcement said the units contain 21 sensors that monitor cleanliness, usage and potential misuse while maintaining user privacy.

The city's subsequent pilot feedback also showed at least one user raising concerns about the time restriction. In Long Beach's published community survey responses, one respondent said the city should increase the limit after nearly being caught inside when time expired.

"Please make it more than ten minutes. I was almost embarrassed in front of strangers still using the restroom," the respondent said.

Mamdani said New York City has roughly one public toilet for every 8,500 residents and characterized the 17 units as a first step toward a larger network. When asked about the restriction Wednesday, he offered a more succinct warning to New Yorkers accustomed to lingering in the bathroom.

"This is not a place to scroll on your phone. I know that many people do that. This isn't one of them," Mamdani said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Bijan Robinson believes Texas' comeback over Ohio State can change entire season trajectory
item.description: Bijan Robinson revealed the Steve Sarkisian halftime moment that told him the Texas Longhorns were about to rally against Ohio State in Austin.
item.content:encoded:
The Texas Longhorns vaulted up the AP poll this week following a thrilling second-half comeback against then-No. 1 Ohio State—a game that still has Atlanta Falcons star Bijan Robinson smiling ear to ear.

Robinson starred for the Longhorns before being taken by the Falcons in the first round of the NFL Draft, and though he was anxiously waiting for his own start to the NFL regular season, he was tapped in this past Saturday night to see how his alma mater would fare at home in Austin, Texas against the Buckeyes.

It didn’t start at all the way Robinson and Longhorns fans wished, but he noticed something in former head coach Steve Sarkisian that gave him hope the second half would be one to remember.

"I knew when Sark ran off because the interview was taking too long or whatever, I knew exactly where his mind went," Robinson told OutKick, while also highlighting his partnership with Sonic. "He had to get back [to the locker room]. He doesn’t have that much time, so he has to get back there as fast as possible, and he’s already game planning in his head for the second half.

"So, I knew something was going to change in that second half."

Whatever changes Sarkisian made worked, and it was quarterback Arch Manning and the Longhorns’ offense going to work as the defense shut down Ohio State star receiver Jeremiah Smith and allowed their teammates to get the ball back.

In the end, Texas scored 21 points in the fourth quarter, including the decisive touchdown and extra point to win, 24-23, in a game that Robinson believes could be season-altering.

"That can change everything," he said. "That can change the whole trajectory of the season. That one half can change everything, and I think just confidence wise, it’s a confidence booster doing that against the number one team in the country. Just knowing we can be in any game, and we can do it against the best team, that’s elite confidence.

"But I think now it’s us understanding every team is trying to come to win, come to beat us and we can’t lose that edge. If we lose the edge, somebody’s going to try to come in and beat us. So, I think it’s a really great start, but we have a long season."

As Robinson said, with the No. 1 team title now, the target is certainly on the backs of the Longhorns moving forward. But as the saying goes, "Pressure is a privilege," and that’s the mindset he thinks his former college squad will have throughout the season as they hope to get back to the College Football Playoff and make a run to the national championship.

"Everybody was texting me after the game. It’s cool to be a part of Texas and the football team," Robinson added. "People text me like I’m on the team. I am a part of the team, but I just give all those guys credit on the field. They played their butts off, man."

With football season officially back, Robinson highlighted his favorite food pairing if he were the one sitting down to watch the Falcons and the rest of the NFL slate on Sundays.

But overall, Robinson loves how great and affordable this special deal is for everyone, especially those families looking for something good to pair with their football each week.

"I feel like it gives everybody an opportunity to get a meal together as a family and they don’t gotta worry about it costing too much, or stuff like that," he said. "They know they can go right to Sonic, order the $7 Big Deal Meal and enjoy it. They can have a full meal and it’s not just a hamburger or a drink or something like that. They can enjoy something together as a family.

"It’s been great to hear the feedback, and all my friends literally went the day they saw it."

item.title: High stakes, social media barbs remind college football fans that Auburn and Florida share history of hatred
item.description: Auburn and Florida renew their 84-game rivalry as new head coaches Alex Golesh and Jon Sumrall face off in their first SEC game Saturday night.
